opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think the answer is more subtle than it first appears.

The numbers look very large when you compare total compute. But you have to ask: where does that compute actually go? At the big companies, a huge fraction goes to inference, because they have products with many users. Another large fraction goes to the frontier training runs themselves, which are enormous. Then there's a lot of engineering and product work, many different modalities, many parallel efforts. So when you look at what's left for genuine research, for testing new ideas, the gap becomes much smaller than the headline numbers suggest.

The second point is about what research actually requires. If you are doing something different, you don't necessarily need the absolute maximum compute to prove it out. You need enough to convince yourself, and others, that an idea is real. Historically, many of the most important ideas in deep learning were demonstrated with a modest amount of compute. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The original transformer used a handful. Even early scaling work was not done at frontier scale. Compute matters a great deal, of course, but for research, ideas are often the bottleneck, not compute.

And I think we're moving into a period where that's increasingly true. For a while, scaling was the recipe. Everyone knew what to do: get more data, more compute, bigger model. It was very low risk, and that's why companies loved it. But when everyone follows the same recipe, you get many companies doing very similar things. Now pre-training data is finite, and the question becomes what to do next, and that's a research question again. In that kind of world, having a clear point of view about what to try matters more than having the most GPUs.

So my assessment is that we have sufficient compute for the research we want to do. We're not trying to win on scale of experimentation. We're trying to do things differently, and if the ideas are correct, I think that will become apparent.

r001.rationale: The response says large companies spread compute across inference, frontier training, engineering and product work, multiple modalities, and parallel efforts, leaving less for research.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response in Ilya's voice, from the conversation history alone.

Well, I think the question presupposes something that I'm not sure is true, which is that the main bottleneck right now is experimental compute. If you look at what the big labs are doing, they're mostly scaling the same recipe. And when everyone is running the same recipe, more compute gives you a better version of the same thing. It doesn't necessarily give you a different thing.

The way I think about it is this. There was a period, call it 2020 to 2025, where the right strategy was to scale. The recipe was known, and the question was mostly who could execute it at the largest scale. That's a game where compute really matters, and I would not want to compete in that game with a smaller budget. But I think we are moving back into an age of research. The recipe for the next thing is not known. And when the recipe is not known, what you need is good ideas and the ability to test them, and testing an idea does not require the largest cluster in the world. It requires enough compute to get a clear signal, and then taste, and then the discipline to actually follow what the experiments tell you rather than what you hoped they would tell you.

I'll put it another way. Having a very large experimental budget can actually be a bit of a trap, because it lets you avoid thinking. You can just try everything. And in a regime where the ideas matter more than the scale, the team that is forced to be careful about which experiments to run may end up ahead, because it's forced to understand.

Now, I don't want to be too romantic about this. Compute matters. If we had ten times more, we would use it, and we would learn faster. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But the advantage of the large labs is real mostly in one direction, which is producing the product that exists today at a larger scale. In the direction of finding what comes next, I think the advantage is much smaller than it looks from the outside, and that is the direction we care about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses large labs using more compute and trying many experiments, but does not explain that their training compute is fragmented across many different work streams.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a real advantage. If you have more compute, you can run more experiments, and you can test ideas at a scale where the answer may be different from what you see in a small experiment. That matters.

But the question is: what experiments do you run? Research isn’t simply a process where you put in compute and get out discoveries. You have some hypothesis about what’s missing, you run an experiment, and then you have to interpret the result. Sometimes a failed experiment tells you the idea is wrong. Sometimes it tells you that you didn’t implement the idea correctly. That judgment is very important.

So I would distinguish between pursuing a direction that’s already established and trying to find a new direction. In the first case, having vastly more compute is an enormous advantage. In the second case, it still helps, but there is much more room for a small group with a good idea. You don’t need to run every possible experiment. You need to run the experiments that let you figure out something important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the advantage of having more compute and choosing experiments, but does not say that larger companies’ training compute is fragmented across different work streams.

sol-6.1.text:
A larger compute budget is certainly an advantage. You can run more experiments, and you can test ideas at a scale where their effects might become clearer. I wouldn’t dismiss that.

But the value of an experiment depends on the question you’re asking. If everyone is pursuing roughly the same direction, then having more compute is a very substantial advantage. If you have a different idea, you may be able to learn something important with a much smaller experiment.

So the question for us is whether we can identify ideas whose promise we can establish with the resources we have. That doesn’t make compute irrelevant. Eventually, you need to scale. But there’s room for research judgment to make a large difference.

r001.rationale: The response says larger budgets allow more experiments and larger-scale tests, but it does not explain that compute is fragmented across companies’ many work streams.
